## Let us begin with a test {.question-slide}

::: {.sentence}
“I saw the man with the telescope.”
:::

::: {.big-question}
Who has the telescope?
:::

::: {.fragment .answer}
The sentence does not say. Humans notice the ambiguity immediately.
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Language is easy to use—and surprisingly difficult to formalize.
:::

::: {.notes}
Do not define NLP yet. Ask students to draw the two interpretations or act them out. 3 minutes.
:::

## Another tiny test

:::: {.challenge-grid .wide}
::: {.challenge}
`This course is sick!`
:::
::: {.challenge}
`This student is sick.`
:::
::: {.challenge}
`The model is sick.`
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .big-question}
Does **sick** mean the same thing each time?
:::

::: {.fragment .answer}
Meaning depends on context, speaker, community, and task.
:::

## So, what is NLP?

::: {.definition}
**Natural Language Processing** studies computational methods for working with human language.
:::

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .chars}
<div class="card-title">Understand</div>

classify · extract · infer
:::
::: {.card .words}
<div class="card-title">Transform</div>

translate · summarize · retrieve
:::
::: {.card .subwords}
<div class="card-title">Generate</div>

answer · assist · converse
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
NLP lives where **language**, **computation**, and **real decisions** meet.
:::

# NLP tasks {.section-slide}

## NLP is not one problem

::: {.task-map}
<div class="task-center">LANGUAGE</div>
<div class="task-node n1">Classify</div><div class="task-node n2">Extract</div>
<div class="task-node n3">Search</div><div class="task-node n4">Translate</div>
<div class="task-node n5">Summarize</div><div class="task-node n6">Generate</div>
<div class="task-node n7">Answer</div><div class="task-node n8">Speak</div>
:::

::: {.takeaway}
The shared material is human language. The **goal** determines what matters.
:::

## One message, many questions

::: {.sentence}
“The battery lasts all day, but the camera struggles at night.”
:::

::: {.fragment .task-outputs}
<div><strong>Sentiment</strong><span>Mixed</span></div>
<div><strong>Extraction</strong><span>battery · camera</span></div>
<div><strong>Summary</strong><span>Great battery, weak night camera</span></div>
<div><strong>Retrieval</strong><span>Find phones with better night photography</span></div>
:::

## You choose the task {.question-slide}

::: {.sentence}
“My flight was cancelled again. I need to be in Rabat tomorrow.”
:::

What could a useful NLP system produce?

:::: {.fragment .challenge-grid .wide}
::: {.challenge}
**Intent**

rebook flight
:::
::: {.challenge}
**Emotion**

frustration
:::
::: {.challenge}
**Response**

offer actionable options
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Invite outputs beyond these three. Ask which errors would be costly. This opens the evaluation theme. 4 minutes.
:::

## Inputs and outputs can both be language

::: {.io-grid}
<div><strong>Text → label</strong><span>spam detection</span></div>
<div><strong>Text → spans</strong><span>named entities</span></div>
<div><strong>Text → text</strong><span>translation</span></div>
<div><strong>Question + documents → answer</strong><span>retrieval QA</span></div>
<div><strong>Audio → text</strong><span>speech recognition</span></div>
<div><strong>Text + image → text</strong><span>multimodal assistance</span></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Before selecting a model, define the input, the desired output, and what counts as success.
:::

# One problem, three eras {.section-slide}

## Our running example

::: {.sentence}
“The screen is beautiful, but the battery is not good.”
:::

::: {.big-question}
Positive or negative?
:::

::: {.fragment .answer}
The task stays fixed. What changes is **where the knowledge comes from**.
:::

## Era I · Write the rules

::: {.rule-sheet}
<div><code>beautiful</code><strong>+1</strong></div>
<div><code>good</code><strong>+1</strong></div>
<div><code>not + positive</code><strong>reverse</strong></div>
<div><code>but</code><strong>emphasize what follows</strong></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Human experts put knowledge directly into patterns, lexicons, and grammars.
:::

## Rules: precise but brittle

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.mini-card}
**Why we like them**

Transparent · controllable · little data · excellent in a narrow stable domain
:::
::: {.mini-card .rule-fail}
**Where they break**

Coverage · exceptions · maintenance · context · changing language
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .sentence}
“The battery is **bad**.” → negative  
“The battery is **badass**.” → ?
:::

## Era II · Learn weights from examples

:::: {.journey}
::: {.stage}
**LABELED TEXT**

reviews + answers
:::
::: {.arrow}
→
:::
::: {.stage .active}
**FEATURES**

counts · n-grams
:::
::: {.arrow}
→
:::
::: {.stage}
**LEARNING**

estimate weights
:::
::: {.arrow}
→
:::
::: {.stage}
**PREDICTION**

apply to new text
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
We stop writing every rule. The model discovers predictive regularities in data.
:::

## A bag of words sees evidence

::: {.feature-weights}
<span class="positive">beautiful +2.1</span>
<span class="positive">excellent +2.8</span>
<span class="negative">poor −2.3</span>
<span class="negative">not −0.9</span>
<span class="neutral">screen +0.1</span>
<span class="neutral">battery −0.1</span>
:::

::: {.fragment .big-equation}
score = evidence from features → probability → label
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway .danger}
But counts alone do not naturally understand why **not good** differs from **good**.
:::

## Era III · Learn representations

:::: {.journey}
::: {.stage}
**MASSIVE TEXT**

broad pretraining
:::
::: {.arrow}
→
:::
::: {.stage .active}
**TRANSFORMER**

contextual representations
:::
::: {.arrow}
→
:::
::: {.stage}
**ADAPT**

fine-tune · prompt
:::
::: {.arrow}
→
:::
::: {.stage}
**TASK**

reuse knowledge
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
The model learns both useful features and how to combine them in context.
:::

## Context changes representation

:::: {.challenge-grid .wide}
::: {.challenge}
river **bank**
:::
::: {.challenge}
central **bank**
:::
::: {.challenge}
bank the airplane
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .answer}
A contextual model can give the same written word a different representation in each sentence.
:::

## Did the newest era “win”? {.question-slide}

| If you need… | Consider… |
|---|---|
| a transparent rule in a stable domain | rules |
| a fast, strong, auditable baseline | statistical learning |
| transfer, context, and broad capability | pretrained Transformers |

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
The best method is the simplest one whose assumptions fit the problem and whose errors are acceptable.
:::

## Checkpoint: where does knowledge live?

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .chars}
<div class="card-title">Rules</div>

In the expert's specification
:::
::: {.card .words}
<div class="card-title">Statistical</div>

In labeled examples and engineered features
:::
::: {.card .subwords}
<div class="card-title">Neural / Transformer</div>

In learned representations, pretraining, and adaptation
:::
::::

# Breakthroughs {.section-slide}

## NLP moved one bottleneck at a time

::: {.history-line}
<div><strong>Rules</strong><span>specify knowledge</span></div>
<div><strong>Statistics</strong><span>learn weights</span></div>
<div><strong>Embeddings</strong><span>learn similarity</span></div>
<div><strong>Sequences</strong><span>model order</span></div>
<div><strong>Attention</strong><span>connect distant words</span></div>
<div><strong>Transformers</strong><span>scale pretraining</span></div>
<div><strong>LLM systems</strong><span>instructions · retrieval · tools</span></div>
:::

## 2013 · Meaning becomes geometry

::: {.semantic-map .large-map}
<span class="cluster-label royalty-label">royalty</span>
<span class="point royal king">king</span>
<span class="point royal queen">queen</span>
<span class="point royal prince">prince</span>
<span class="point human man">man</span>
<span class="point human woman">woman</span>
<span class="point fruit apple">apple</span>
<span class="point fruit banana">banana</span>
<span class="point fruit orange">orange</span>
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Distributed representations let related words share statistical strength.
:::

## 2014–2017 · Attention changes the route

::: {.attention-demo}
<div class="source">The animal didn't cross the street because <mark>it</mark> was tired.</div>
<div class="attention-arrow">↑</div>
<div class="attention-target">animal</div>
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Instead of compressing a whole sequence into one state, a model can look directly at relevant positions.
:::

<div class="citation">The Transformer made attention central and enabled highly parallel training [@vaswani2017attention].</div>

## Pretraining changes the economics

::: {.pretrain-tree}
<div class="trunk">GENERAL LANGUAGE MODEL<br><small>learn once from broad text</small></div>
<div class="branches">
<span>Translate</span><span>Classify</span><span>Summarize</span><span>Answer</span><span>Extract</span>
</div>
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
One broad model can be adapted to many downstream tasks.
:::

## Today · The model becomes a system

::: {.system-orbit}
<div class="orbit-center">LANGUAGE<br>MODEL</div>
<div class="orbit-item oi1">Search</div><div class="orbit-item oi2">Tools</div>
<div class="orbit-item oi3">Documents</div><div class="orbit-item oi4">Images</div>
<div class="orbit-item oi5">Memory</div><div class="orbit-item oi6">Evaluation</div>
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Modern applications combine models with retrieval, tools, interfaces, and safeguards.
:::

## Fluency is not evidence

::: {.big-question}
A confident answer can still be wrong.
:::

:::: {.fragment .challenge-grid .wide}
::: {.challenge}
**Hallucination**

unsupported claims
:::
::: {.challenge}
**Bias**

patterns inherited from data
:::
::: {.challenge}
**Drift**

knowledge becomes outdated
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .warning}
Throughout this course, evaluation and error analysis matter as much as architecture.
:::
